title: Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment (Strengthening the Safety Net) Bill 2023
short_title: Social Services and Other Legislation Amendment (Strengthening the Safety Net) Bill 2023

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: The bill would increase several social security payments for people on low incomes.

It would raise the age limit for single parents to receive Parenting Payment Single, increase working-age and student payments, expand JobSeeker Payment eligibility for older recipients, and boost Commonwealth Rent Assistance.

The changes include raising the youngest child age for Parenting Payment Single from under 8 to under 14 years, adding $40 per fortnight to various payments, lowering the qualifying age for the higher JobSeeker rate to 55 years, and increasing rent assistance by 15 per cent.
changes: Expanding Parenting Payment Single to single principal carers with a youngest child under 14 years.
Increasing working-age and student payments by $40 per fortnight.
Lowering the age for the higher JobSeeker Payment rate to 55 years after nine continuous months on payment.
Raising Commonwealth Rent Assistance maximum rates by 15 per cent.
summary.affected: Single parents, jobseekers, students, disability support pensioners (youth), and rent assistance recipients.

Yes, a job is the best way to improve the living standards of individuals and their families, but I'd say it's a little hard to look for a job if you're starving, cold or can't afford transport. In my view, $40 a fortnight, while a step in the right direction, is not enough and falls short of the coalition's increase of $50 a fortnight in 2021. Whilst I note the government has a fine line to walk between addressing the cost-of-living challenges and addressing inflation, I don't believe that providing this minimal increase to income support, which still falls chronically below the poverty line, is the right approach, nor is it living Labor's own values, particularly as they've promised time and again not to leave any Australian behind.* ### Amendment text > *That all words after "That" be omitted with a view to substituting the following words:* > > *"whilst not declining to give the bill a second reading, the House:* > > *(1) notes:* > >> *(a) while in Government, the Coalition through disciplined economic management was able to deliver the largest permanent increase to the JobSeeker income support payment;* >> >

The majority voted against [amendments and requests](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2023-08-02.18.1) introduced by South Australian Senator [Anne Ruston](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/sa/anne_ruston) (Liberal), which means they were unsuccessful. ### What do these amendments do? Senator Ruston [explained that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2023-08-02.18.1): > *The coalition's amendment and request remove the $40 increase per fortnight for JobSeeker and related working-age payments and replaces it with an increase to the income-free areas of $150 per fortnight. These payments include JobSeeker, disability support pension under 21, youth allowance, Austudy payment and parenting payment partner.*

The majority voted against an [amendment](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2023-08-02.39.1) introduced by Victorian Senator [Janet Rice](https://theyvoteforyou.org.au/people/senate/victoria/janet_rice) (Greens), which means it failed. ### What does the amendment do? Senator Rice [explained that](https://www.openaustralia.org.au/senate/?gid=2023-08-02.39.1): > *This amendment is about implementing one of the recommendations from the Royal Commission into the Robodebt Scheme ...* > > *We have legislation before us today to amend the Social Security Act. It is a very straightforward thing, as per my amendment, to reinstate the provisions that were there before the Abbott government's changes. This recommendation isn't complex. It's not one of the complex robodebt royal commission recommendations. I understand the arguments from the government that we need to implement those recommendations slowly and carefully. I accept that for most of them, but that's not the case for this one ...* > > *In the meantime, here is a very straightforward opportunity to provide some justice for people by putting in place the provision as it used to be—to say that debts that are more than six years old should not be pursued. We don't know when the full suite of changes, after the government's careful consideration of them, are going to come into place. It might be years off. In the meantime, at least do this. It was a very simple recommendation of the royal commission and it's something that could easily be done today.*
